description: We are a group of 6 best friends from secondary school and we had great fun completing this hackathon! Our project - Sky of Selena - is the culmination of 2 days of no sleep work and we are very proud of our project :)
summary: We developed the Lunar Landing Site Navigator, an interactive web application and core computational engine that evaluates and compares candidate landing sites for lunar missions around the rugged lunar south pole. Near the poles, extreme topography creates a challenging environment where crater rims can block vital sunlight for solar power generation, while lunar libration causes the Earth to shift across the horizon, interacting with local terrain to control direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows. Our application addresses this challenge by combining NASA’s astronomical ephemerides data and Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) with 3D vector geometry. Through automated horizon ray-casting and vector dot products, our software simulates precise temporal windows of solar illumination and communication availability. Users can explore these results through interactive maps, timeline charts, and skyline profile views. This project is important as it reduces mission risk by turning raw lunar elevation data and orbital mechanics into clear visibility windows, helping mission planners avoid power-draining shadow traps and communication blackouts.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive mission-planning platform built to evaluate and compare candidate landing sites around the Moon's south pole.

Landing near the lunar south pole requires a consideration of two key factors. Because the Sun sits permanently low on the horizon, towering crater rims cast massive shadows that can starve solar-powered landers of sunlight for energy. At the same time, the Earth hovers just above the horizon, meaning slight wobbles in the Moon's orbit (lunar libration) can cause Earth to dip behind mountains, which can cut off direct communication.

Our platform solves this by turning raw NASA topography and orbital data into clear, visual mission forecasts through three connected components:

  • Automated Terrain Mapping (Python Pipeline): Using elevation maps from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA), our pipeline scans 360 degrees around candidate landing sites to map out every surrounding crater rim and ridge, creating a complete local horizon skyline profile.
  • Visibility & Power Engine (TypeScript Core): Combining NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data with 3D vector geometry, our engine tracks the exact positions of the Sun and Earth over time. It checks when both clear the local terrain horizon, calculates how directly sunlight hits sloped ground, and flags safe windows for power generation and direct-to-Earth communication.
  • Interactive Mission Dashboard (React Web App): Users can explore candidate sites—like Shackleton Rim, Malapert Massif, and Haworth—through interactive polar maps, horizon skyline views, and timeline charts to compare power and communication uptime side by side.



Key Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Prevents Mission-Ending Hazards: Gives mission planners clear foresight to keep rovers, landers, and future Artemis habitats out of power-draining shadow traps and unexpected communication blackouts.
  • Instant Decision-Making: By pre-computing heavy 360-degree terrain scans into lightweight site profiles, engineers can compare complex polar locations instantaneously in their browser without needing specialised GIS software.
  • Holistic Trade-Off Analysis: Instead of analysing sunlight and communications separately, our platform overlays them in the same timeline, making it easy to spot landing zones where continuous power from the Sun and direct-to-Earth communication overlap.

Tools, Languages & Data Used

  • Frontend & UI: TypeScript, React, JavaScript, Vite
  • Core Calculation Engine: Node.js, custom 3D geometry & ephemeris modules
  • Data Processing: Python (rasterio, numpy, scipy)
  • NASA & Partner Data: NASA LRO LOLA Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), NASA JPL Horizons Ephemerides (DE441), and SELENE Kaguya topography datasets

How Our Project Is Creative

  • Visualizing Complex Orbital Mechanics: Rather than presenting users with raw coordinate tables or static elevation rasters, we designed the interface to translate 3D vector geometry and terrain masking into interactive polar skyline profiles and temporal visibility charts, allowing mission planners to immediately interpret how local topography shapes power and communication availability.
  • Interactive Landing Simulator: The game transforms lunar and Martian exploration into an interactive simulator, allowing users to experience the challenges faced during landings. The combination of realistic physics, dynamic environmental hazards and full control to the user creates a both educational and entertaining experience.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Astrophysical Fidelity at the Poles: Simplified lighting models often fail near the lunar poles because the Moon’s low axial tilt keeps the Sun near the horizon, while lunar libration causes Earth’s apparent position to shift across the sky. We accounted for both phenomena using NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data so that calculated illumination and direct-to-Earth communication windows reflect true orbital conditions.
  • Computational Architecture and Responsiveness: Performing 360-degree horizon ray-casting across high-resolution Digital Elevation Models is computationally intensive and would introduce significant latency if executed client-side. To maintain responsiveness without sacrificing terrain resolution, we decoupled the architecture, executing the heavy ray-casting offline in Python and serving pre-computed horizon profiles and ephemeris baselines to the browser for interactive visibility and power analysis across simulated mission timelines.
